items.prompt: Which planet is closest to the Sun?

options.label: Earth
Venus
Mercury
Mars

rubric: Mercury orbits closest to the Sun.
Venus is a common wrong guess because it is bright and nearby.

items.prompt: What is the name of the galaxy that contains our Solar System?

options.label: Andromeda
Whirlpool
Milky Way
Triangulum

rubric: Our Solar System lies in the Milky Way.
Andromeda is the nearest large galaxy, often confused with ours.

items.prompt: What type of object is the Sun?

options.label: A star
A planet
A comet
A nebula

rubric: The Sun is a star.
Other options are different classes of objects.

items.prompt: Which term names the path an object takes around a star or planet?

options.label: Orbit
Rotation
Phase
Eclipse

rubric: An orbit is the path around another body.
Rotation is spin about an own axis, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: What unit is defined as the distance light travels in one year?

options.label: Light-year
Parsec per year
Solar radius
Astronomical unit

rubric: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year.
The astronomical unit is the Earth-Sun distance, often confused.

items.prompt: Which of the following are planets in our Solar System? Select all that apply.

options.label: Ceres
Saturn
Neptune
Pluto

rubric: Neptune and Saturn are planets.
Pluto and Ceres are dwarf planets, which learners often count as planets.

items.prompt: A student is reading a book about stars. It says a star ends its life as a white dwarf after exhausting its fuel and shedding outer layers. The student wants to recall which star type this describes. Which kind of star typically ends its life as a white dwarf?

options.label: A newly forming protostar
A star far more massive than the Sun
A star made only of iron
A Sun-like star of modest mass

rubric: Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs.
Very massive stars end as neutron stars or black holes.

items.prompt: Why do we have seasons on Earth?

options.label: Earth moves much closer to the Sun in summer
Earth's axis is tilted as it orbits the Sun
The Sun's output changes with the months
The Moon blocks sunlight in winter

rubric: Axial tilt changes sunlight angle and day length.
Distance explanation is a very common misconception.

items.prompt: Why does the Moon show different phases during a month?

options.label: Earth's shadow covers parts of it
Clouds hide parts of it
We see different amounts of its sunlit half
It changes its own brightness

rubric: Phases come from viewing angle of the sunlit half.
Earth's shadow causes eclipses, not phases.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why stars appear to rise and set each night?

options.label: Stars orbit Earth once a day
The Sun drags stars along
Earth rotates on its axis
Stars move closer and farther

rubric: Earth's rotation causes the apparent motion.
Stars do not circle Earth daily.

items.prompt: Which best describes how a star shines for most of its life?

options.label: It splits heavy atoms in its core
It reflects light from nearby stars
It fuses hydrogen into helium in its core
It burns chemically like a fire

rubric: Main sequence stars fuse hydrogen to helium.
Burning and fission are common misconceptions.

items.prompt: Which pair correctly classifies the objects as a planet type?

options.label: Mercury and Uranus are ice dwarfs
Mars and Venus are gas giants
Earth and Neptune are rocky
Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants

rubric: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.
Other options mismatch planet types.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why a solar eclipse is only seen from part of Earth? Select all that apply.

options.label: The Sun briefly turns off its light
The Moon's shadow is small where it reaches Earth
The Moon passes between the Sun and Earth
Earth's shadow falls across the Moon

rubric: Moon between Sun and Earth casts a small shadow.
Earth's shadow describes a lunar eclipse.

items.prompt: A learner notices that the Sun looks far larger and brighter than other stars at night. A friend says the Sun must be the biggest star there is. Which explanation is best?

options.label: Other stars are all smaller planets
The Sun gives out more light than any star
The Sun is just much closer than other stars
The Sun is the largest star known

rubric: Distance explains the Sun's apparent size and brightness.
Many stars are larger or more luminous than the Sun.

items.prompt: What is the main reason Earth has seasons?

options.label: Earth's distance from the Sun is smallest in summer and largest in winter
The Sun's energy output rises in summer and falls in winter every single year
Earth's own shadow covers the winter hemisphere more because of its orbit shape
Earth's axis is tilted, so sunlight strikes each hemisphere more directly in its summer

rubric: Axial tilt changes the angle and length of daylight over the year.
The distance idea is a common misconception; Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.

items.prompt: What causes the phases of the Moon?

options.label: The Moon's own light output rises and falls in a regular monthly cycle
As the Moon orbits Earth, we see a changing fraction of its sunlit half
Earth's shadow covers different fractions of the Moon through each month
Clouds and dust in Earth's atmosphere hide parts of the Moon each night

rubric: Half the Moon is always lit; our viewing angle changes as it orbits.
The shadow idea confuses phases with lunar eclipses.

items.prompt: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon from Earth?

options.label: The Moon does not rotate at all, so one side always points toward us
The Moon rotates once in the same time it takes to orbit Earth once
Earth's magnetic field locks the Moon's near side toward our planet
The far side is permanently dark, so only the near side is ever visible

rubric: Synchronous rotation: rotation period equals orbital period.
Saying the Moon does not rotate is a frequent misconception; it would then show all its sides.

items.prompt: What does the color of a star mainly tell us?

options.label: Its age only, with blue stars always older than red stars
Its distance from Earth, with red stars farther away than blue stars
Its surface temperature, with blue stars hotter than red stars
Its size only, with blue stars always smaller than red stars

rubric: Color follows surface temperature: blue is hot, red is cool.
Distance, age and size are not read directly from color.

items.prompt: What process makes a main-sequence star such as the Sun shine?

options.label: Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core and releasing energy
Burning chemical fuel such as carbon combining with oxygen in its core
Slowly shrinking under gravity with no nuclear reactions inside
Splitting heavy atoms such as uranium deep inside its core

rubric: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen to helium.
Chemical burning and fission are wrong energy sources and could not last billions of years.

items.prompt: Which statements about the Milky Way are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: The Sun lies in its disk, far from the galactic center
The Sun sits at the center, with other stars orbiting it
It is the only galaxy that exists in the universe
It is a spiral galaxy containing hundreds of billions of stars

rubric: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy and the Sun is in the disk, far from the center.
Distractors reflect Sun-centered and one-galaxy misconceptions.

items.prompt: A student sees a bright point in the evening sky. It twinkles very little, and over several weeks it shifts position against the background stars. The student asks what it most likely is.

options.label: A comet, because anything that changes position against the stars must have a tail
A satellite, because objects moving over weeks must be orbiting only the Earth
A distant star, because all bright points in the night sky are stars that move slowly
A planet, because planets orbit the Sun and look like steady discs that move against the stars

rubric: Planets are nearby, twinkle less and wander against the fixed stars.
Stars keep fixed patterns; comets show tails and satellites cross the sky in minutes.

items.prompt: A planet orbits a Sun-like star at 4 AU. Using Kepler's third law, P^2 = a^3 (P in years, a in AU), what is its orbital period?

options.label: 4 years
2 years
8 years
16 years

rubric: P^2 = 4^3 = 64, so P = 8 years.
16 comes from forgetting the square root; 4 assumes period equals distance.

items.prompt: Light takes about 500 seconds to travel 1 AU. How long does light take to travel from the Sun to an object 1.5 AU away?

options.label: About 8.3 minutes
About 5.6 minutes
About 12.5 minutes
About 750 minutes

rubric: 750 minutes forgets to convert seconds to minutes; 8.3 is the 1 AU time.

items.prompt: A nearby star shows a parallax angle of 0.25 arcseconds. Using d = 1/p (d in parsecs, p in arcseconds), how far away is it?

options.label: 4 parsecs
0.25 parsecs
2 parsecs
0.5 parsecs

rubric: d = 1/0.25 = 4 parsecs.
0.25 repeats the angle; smaller parallax means larger distance, not equal.

items.prompt: Use Hubble's law, v = H0 x d, with H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc. A galaxy is 200 Mpc away. What is its recession speed?

options.label: 270 km/s

rubric: 0.35 comes from dividing instead of multiplying.

items.prompt: Tonight the Moon is full. Using the roughly 29.5-day cycle of phases, what phase will it show about 7 days from now?

options.label: First quarter
New Moon
Waxing gibbous
Last quarter

rubric: After full comes waning gibbous, then last quarter about a week later.
First quarter occurs a week before full; new Moon is about two weeks later.

items.prompt: Stars of 0.5, 1 and 10 solar masses are on the main sequence. Applying the rule that more massive stars burn fuel much faster, which statements follow? Select all that apply.

options.label: The 0.5 solar mass star lives longer than the Sun
The 10 solar mass star has the shortest main-sequence life
All three stars have about the same main-sequence lifetime
The 10 solar mass star lives longest because it has the most fuel

rubric: Massive stars are far more luminous, so they exhaust fuel sooner; low-mass stars last longest.
The most-fuel idea ignores the much faster burning rate.

items.prompt: An observer in the Northern Hemisphere measures the altitude of Polaris above the horizon as 40 degrees. They know that Polaris's altitude is about equal to the observer's latitude. What is their latitude?

options.label: About 40 degrees S
About 50 degrees N
About 40 degrees N
About 90 degrees N

rubric: Polaris altitude is about equal to latitude, so 40 degrees N.
50 uses the complement; 90 is the pole where Polaris is overhead.

items.prompt: An asteroid orbits the Sun with a period of 8 years. Using Kepler's third law (P^2 = a^3, with P in years and a in AU), what is its semi-major axis?

options.label: 8 AU
4 AU
16 AU
2 AU

rubric: a^3 = 64, so a = 4 AU.
Taking the cube root of 8 (giving 2 AU) or skipping the squaring step are the typical slips.

items.prompt: A star shows an annual parallax of 0.25 arcseconds. Given 1 parsec = 3.26 light-years, about how far away is it?

options.label: About 0.8 light-years
About 4 light-years
About 52 light-years
About 13 light-years

rubric: d = 1/p = 4 pc, and 4 x 3.26 is about 13 ly.
Distractors confuse parsecs with light-years or multiply parallax instead of inverting it.

items.prompt: A star has 3 times the Sun's radius and a surface temperature half the Sun's. Using L is proportional to R^2 x T^4, what is its luminosity compared with the Sun?

options.label: About 0.56 times the Sun's
About 1.5 times the Sun's
About 9 times the Sun's
About 4.5 times the Sun's

rubric: Using T^2 or T alone, or ignoring temperature, gives the other values.

items.prompt: At which Moon phase does the Moon rise at about midnight?

options.label: Full Moon
First quarter
New Moon
Last quarter

rubric: Last quarter Moon is 90 degrees west of the Sun, so it rises about six hours before sunrise, near midnight.
First quarter rises near noon, full near sunset, new near sunrise.

items.prompt: Using Hubble's law with H0 = 70 km/s per Mpc, what is the recession velocity of a galaxy 200 Mpc away?

options.label: 350 km/s
2.9 km/s

rubric: Dividing instead of multiplying, or slipping a factor of ten, gives the distractors.

items.prompt: For an observer at latitude 40 degrees North, which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.label: A star at declination +45 degrees is circumpolar.
The celestial equator crosses the meridian 40 degrees above the southern horizon.
A star at declination -55 degrees never rises.
A star at declination +60 degrees is circumpolar.
Polaris sits about 40 degrees above the northern horizon.

rubric: Polaris altitude equals latitude; circumpolar means dec > 90 - 40 = 50; never rises means dec < -50.
Dec +45 is below the 50 degree limit, and the equator crosses the meridian at 90 - 40 = 50 degrees.

items.prompt: Your telescope has a focal length of 1000 mm. With a 25 mm eyepiece you get a 40x view of Jupiter. You want about 100x for a closer look at its moons. Which eyepiece should you use (magnification = telescope focal length / eyepiece focal length)?

options.label: 2.5 mm
40 mm
4 mm
10 mm

rubric: 1000 / 100 = 10 mm eyepiece.
Shorter eyepieces such as 4 mm (250x) overshoot; 40 mm gives lower power.

items.prompt: A student says summer is warm because Earth is closer to the Sun then. Which fact most directly contradicts this explanation?

options.label: Earth's distance from the Sun varies by about 30% over a year
Summer days are longer, so the Sun is always nearer in June
Both hemispheres have summer at the same time of year, worldwide
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, during northern winter

rubric: Perihelion in January falls in northern winter, so distance cannot drive seasons; axial tilt does.
Other options are false claims or do not test the distance idea.

items.prompt: A star has a surface temperature of about 3,500 K, cooler than the Sun, yet it is 1,000 times more luminous. What can you conclude about it?

options.label: It is a Sun-like main-sequence star, since luminosity depends only on temperature
Its radius is far larger than the Sun's, since luminosity also scales with surface area
It is a white dwarf, since very luminous stars are always hot at the surface
Its radius is smaller than the Sun's, since cool surfaces radiate weakly per unit area

rubric: L is proportional to R^2 T^4, so low T with high L requires a huge radius (a red giant or supergiant).
Distractors ignore the radius term or misclassify the star.

items.prompt: A 10-solar-mass star has far more hydrogen than the Sun but a much shorter main-sequence life. What best explains this?

options.label: Its luminosity rises much faster than its mass, so it uses up hydrogen sooner
Its core holds less hydrogen per unit mass, so its fuel runs out early
Its stronger gravity makes it collapse after a fixed time whatever the fuel
It fuses helium from the start, which releases energy faster than hydrogen

rubric: Lifetime is proportional to fuel / burn rate, and burn rate rises roughly as M^3.5, so lifetime falls.
Distractors misstate the fuel content or the fusion stage.

items.prompt: A student reasons: 'A planet with 0.1 of its star's radius blocks 10% of the starlight, so transit depth = Rp/Rs.' What is wrong with this step?

options.label: Depth depends on the diameter of the disk, so it is 2Rp/Rs, which is 20%
Depth depends on the mass ratio, so the planet's mass must be known
Depth depends on the volume ratio, so it is (Rp/Rs)^3, which is 0.1%
Depth depends on the area ratio, so it is (Rp/Rs)^2, which is 1%

rubric: The planet blocks a disk of area pi Rp^2 out of pi Rs^2, giving (Rp/Rs)^2.
Cubing, doubling, or using mass misidentifies what is blocked.

items.prompt: Why does a lunar eclipse not occur at every full Moon?

options.label: Earth's shadow is too short to reach the Moon except when the Moon is at perigee
The Moon is full only when it is farthest from Earth, which places it outside the shadow
Earth's 23.5 degree axial tilt shifts the shadow away from the Moon in most months
The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5 degrees, so it usually passes above or below Earth's shadow

rubric: The orbital inclination means alignment with the shadow happens only near the nodes.
Axial tilt and shadow length are not the cause; the shadow is long enough to cover the Moon.

items.prompt: Which observations are used as evidence for dark matter? Select all that apply.

options.label: Nearby stars show an annual parallax shift
Gravitational lensing by clusters exceeds what visible mass explains
Galaxies in clusters move faster than visible mass can bind
Spiral galaxy rotation curves stay flat far from the centre
Redshift increases roughly linearly with galaxy distance

rubric: Flat rotation curves, excess lensing and fast cluster motions all imply unseen mass.
Hubble's law shows expansion and parallax gives distance; neither indicates dark matter.

items.prompt: Two stars, A and B, look equally bright in the night sky. Parallax measurements show B's parallax is half of A's. You compare their true luminosities using the inverse-square law.

options.label: B is about 4 times as luminous as A
They have the same luminosity
B is about 2 times as luminous as A
A is about 4 times as luminous as B

rubric: Half the parallax means twice the distance, and equal apparent brightness then requires 2^2 = 4 times the luminosity.
Using a linear rather than squared relation gives 2; reversing the distance ratio favours A.

items.prompt: Stars A and B appear equally bright in the sky, and dust is negligible. A's parallax angle is half of B's. How does A's luminosity compare with B's?

options.label: One quarter of B's luminosity
2 times B's luminosity
4 times B's luminosity
Equal to B's luminosity

rubric: Half the parallax means twice the distance, and luminosity scales with distance squared at equal apparent brightness, so A is 4 times as luminous.
Choosing 2 forgets that flux falls off as the square of distance.

items.prompt: Venus appears largest in a telescope when it is a thin crescent. What best explains this?

options.label: Its thick atmosphere swells when it faces away from the Sun, which enlarges the disk
It is then on the far side of the Sun, so sunlight strikes it at a grazing angle
Earth's shadow then covers most of its disk, which leaves only a thin lit crescent visible
It is then nearest Earth, between us and the Sun, so its disk is large but mostly unlit

rubric: At inferior conjunction Venus is closest and its night side faces us, giving a large crescent.
Earth's shadow never falls on Venus, and the far-side position gives a small full disk, not a crescent.

items.prompt: A star has a surface temperature near 3,200 K and a luminosity about 10,000 times the Sun's. What does this combination imply about the star?

options.label: It has a very small radius, since cool surfaces must be compact to give such a high output
It is a main-sequence red dwarf, since all cool stars are low in mass and luminosity
It has a very large radius, since luminosity scales with surface area times temperature^4
It is a white dwarf, since its red colour shows that fusion has ended in the core

rubric: A cool surface radiates little per unit area, so 10,000 solar luminosities requires a huge area: a red giant or supergiant.
Red dwarfs are faint and white dwarfs are hot and tiny; the small-radius option reverses the scaling.

items.prompt: We always see the same face of the Moon from Earth. Which statement correctly diagnoses why?

options.label: The Moon's far side is permanently dark, so we can never see that part of its surface lit
The Moon rotates once per Earth day, so the same side faces us at the same time each night
The Moon rotates once per orbit, so its rotation period equals its orbital period
The Moon does not rotate at all, so one face stays pointed toward Earth as it orbits

rubric: Synchronous rotation means one spin per orbit, keeping one face toward Earth.
A non-rotating Moon would show all its faces over one orbit; the far side is lit as often as the near side.

items.prompt: Stars far from the centre of a spiral galaxy orbit at roughly constant speed instead of slowing with distance. What would visible mass alone predict, and what does the flat curve imply?

options.label: Speeds should stay flat; the curves match the visible mass and need no extra component
Speeds should fall with distance; flat curves suggest extra unseen mass extending outward
Speeds should rise with distance; flat curves suggest the visible disk is lighter than thought
Speeds should fall with distance; flat curves suggest stars are accelerated by galactic winds

rubric: With mass concentrated centrally, orbital speeds should decline like a Keplerian system; flat curves point to extended unseen mass.
Other options misstate the expected trend or invoke an unsupported force.

items.prompt: Which observations are independent lines of evidence for a universe that was hot and dense and has expanded since? Select all that apply.

options.label: Helium making up roughly a quarter of ordinary matter by mass in primordial gas
The 11-year cycle of sunspot numbers on the Sun
The heavily cratered far side of the Moon
A nearly uniform microwave background at about 2.7 K
Spectral lines of distant galaxies shifted to longer wavelengths in proportion to distance

rubric: The CMB, primordial helium abundance and the redshift-distance relation each follow from a hot expanding early universe.
Lunar craters and sunspot cycles concern local bodies and say nothing about cosmic history.

items.prompt: A star's brightness drops by 1% with a flat-bottomed dip every 3.2 days. Its measured radial velocity also shifts back and forth with the same 3.2-day period. Which interpretation best fits both observations together?

options.label: A dark starspot rotating into view, which would dim the star but not shift its radial velocity periodically
An eclipsing pair of near-equal stars, which would give much deeper dips and large velocity swings
A planet transiting the star, whose orbit also tugs the star and causes the periodic velocity shift
Radial pulsation like a Cepheid, which would give a smooth, rounded brightness variation, not flat dips

rubric: A flat-bottomed 1% dip with a matching velocity wobble indicates a transiting planet seen via both methods.
Spots and pulsations do not give flat dips with matched orbital Doppler shifts, and equal stars would give far deeper eclipses.

items.prompt: You need the distance to a galaxy about 200 Mpc away, and the method must work at that range with a calibrated luminosity. Which method best meets these criteria?

options.label: Cepheid period-luminosity relation, since Cepheids can be resolved individually at any distance
Trigonometric parallax, since it is purely geometric and needs no calibration at any distance
Type Ia supernova standard candles, since they are bright enough to see and calibrated nearby
Main-sequence fitting of a nearby cluster, since cluster stars all lie at one distance

rubric: Type Ia supernovae are luminous enough to be seen at hundreds of Mpc and are calibrated with nearer examples.
Parallax is far too small at that range, and individual Cepheids or cluster stars cannot be resolved there.

items.prompt: A student claims summer is hot because Earth is then closest to the Sun. Which evidence most directly refutes this claim?

options.label: Earth's orbit is nearly circular, so distance changes between seasons are too small to matter
The Sun's output varies by only a tiny fraction over a year, so Earth's distance cannot change the heating
Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, and the Southern Hemisphere is in summer at the same time as the Northern winter
Summer days are longer than winter days at every latitude, so day length alone must explain all of the heating

rubric: Opposite seasons in the two hemispheres at the same distance, with perihelion in January, directly contradict a distance explanation.
Other options are partly true or false but do not directly test the claim; day length does not differ at the equator.

items.prompt: With a fixed budget and observing from a dark site, your goal is to see as many faint galaxies as possible. Which instrument best meets this goal?

options.label: A 10 cm telescope with a 3x Barlow lens, because longer effective focal length brightens the image
A 5 cm binocular on a tripod, because two eyes always reveal fainter detail than one
A 20 cm Dobsonian at low magnification, because larger aperture collects more light for dim extended objects
An 8 cm refractor with a 400x eyepiece, because high magnification makes faint galaxies bigger and brighter

rubric: Light gathering grows with aperture area, and low magnification keeps extended objects bright.
Magnification spreads light and dims the image; it does not add light.

items.prompt: A writer claims that the Sun, like every star, will end its life as a supernova. Which critique is best supported by stellar evolution?

options.label: The claim is correct for the Sun's red giant phase, since that phase involves a brief explosive flash
The claim fails because stars of Sun-like mass shed their envelopes and leave a white dwarf
The claim is correct, since all stars end in explosions that return their mass to space
The claim fails because the Sun will fuse iron in its core and then collapse quietly into a black hole

rubric: Core-collapse supernovae need stars above roughly 8 solar masses; the Sun ends as a planetary nebula and white dwarf.
Distractors confuse the red giant stage or the fate of massive stars with the Sun's.

items.prompt: A team reports that a planet orbits within its star's habitable zone and concludes it is therefore habitable. Which critique is best?

options.label: The zone only marks temperatures where liquid water could exist given a suitable atmosphere, which is unknown
The conclusion fails only because habitable zones apply to Sun-like stars and not to any other kind
The conclusion is sound, since a habitable-zone orbit fixes surface temperature and atmosphere together
The conclusion fails because planets in any such zone are always tidally locked and so have no water

rubric: The habitable zone is a necessary orbital condition, not proof; atmosphere, composition and other factors decide habitability.
Orbit does not fix atmosphere, zones exist for other stars, and tidal locking does not preclude water.

items.prompt: A student says: "All galaxies recede from us, so the Milky Way must sit at the centre of the expansion." Which are valid critiques of this claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: Under uniform expansion, an observer in any galaxy sees the same recession pattern
A speed-distance law that is linear can arise only if we are located at the centre
Galaxies recede because the Milky Way's gravity pushes them outward
Expansion adds space between galaxies everywhere, so no privileged centre is needed
Redshift shows that only the nearest galaxies recede while distant ones approach

rubric: Uniform expansion produces the same Hubble-type pattern for every observer, so no centre follows.
Linear recession needs no central location, gravity pulls rather than pushes, and distant galaxies show larger redshifts.

items.prompt: You want a sharp photograph of Jupiter's cloud bands. Criteria: the planet should be as close, as fully lit and as high in the sky as possible. Which plan best meets these criteria?

options.label: Shoot when Jupiter is low on the horizon just after sunset, since the planet looks largest there
Shoot near conjunction, when Jupiter is in the evening twilight and easy to locate
Shoot when Jupiter is at a quarter phase, since shadows then enhance cloud contrast
Shoot near opposition around local midnight, when it is closest, fully lit and highest

rubric: Near opposition Jupiter is nearest Earth and fully illuminated, and at midnight it crosses the meridian at its highest, minimising turbulence.
Conjunction puts it behind the Sun, low altitude adds atmospheric blur, and Jupiter shows almost no phase.

items.prompt: To place a galaxy about 500 Mpc away on the distance scale, you need an indicator that is bright enough to see at that range and calibrated by nearer rungs. Which indicator is best?

options.label: Cepheid variables
Trigonometric parallax
Type Ia supernovae
Main-sequence fitting

rubric: Type Ia supernovae are bright standard candles calibrated with Cepheids, so they reach hundreds of Mpc.
Cepheids and main-sequence fitting fade out far closer, and parallax works only within our own Galaxy.

items.prompt: A writer claims: 'Space is expanding, so Earth's orbit around the Sun grows along with the universe.' Which critique is best?

options.label: Gravitationally bound systems do not expand, because their size is set by local forces rather than the cosmic flow
Expansion acts only on light, stretching photons while leaving all distances between pieces of matter unchanged
Expansion is real but so slow that the orbit grows by an amount far below anything we could measure today
Expansion operates only inside galaxy clusters, where it appears as a small tidal effect on nearby planets

rubric: Bound systems such as the Solar System are held together by gravity, so their sizes are set by local dynamics.
The distractors treat expansion as a tiny effect or as acting only on light or clusters, which misstates the physics.

items.prompt: Which observation most directly shows that most of a cluster's mass is not in its visible stars or hot gas?

options.label: Flat rotation curves of spiral galaxies at large radii, which stay constant well beyond the visible disk
Redshifts of cluster galaxies that follow the smooth Hubble flow with distance from us
A tight Tully-Fisher relation linking a spiral galaxy's luminosity to its rotation speed
Lensing mass peaks that sit offset from the X-ray gas after two clusters collided

rubric: The Bullet Cluster shows lensing mass separated from the dominant baryonic gas, which is direct evidence of unseen mass.
Rotation curves and Tully-Fisher concern single galaxies and can be fitted by alternative gravity, and Hubble flow says nothing about mass.

items.prompt: You want an Earth-size candidate's radius and a first look at its atmosphere, and its orbit is known to be edge-on. Which detection method serves best?

options.label: Transit photometry, since depth gives radius and starlight filtered by the atmosphere carries spectra
Gravitational microlensing, since it detects planets of any orbital alignment around distant stars
Radial velocity monitoring, since it gives a precise minimum mass for planets near the star
Direct imaging with a coronagraph, since it resolves the planet from the glare of its star

rubric: Transits give radius from depth, and transmission spectroscopy reads the atmosphere when the orbit is edge-on.
Radial velocity gives mass, imaging struggles with Earth-size planets, and microlensing events do not repeat for follow-up.

items.prompt: A student says a 2 solar-mass main-sequence star lives about half as long as the Sun because it has twice the fuel. Which critique is best?

options.label: Fuel per unit mass is the same for all stars, so lifetime depends only on surface temperature, and halves for a 2 solar-mass star
Luminosity rises steeply with mass, roughly M^3.5, so lifetime falls roughly as M^-2.5, to under a fifth
Massive stars start burning helium early, which lasts longer than hydrogen burning, so lifetime is similar to the Sun's
Lifetime scales as M^2 because more mass means more hydrogen to burn, so the star lives about four times longer

rubric: Lifetime is roughly fuel divided by luminosity, so M / M^3.5 gives about M^-2.5, near 0.18 for a 2 solar-mass star.
The distractors ignore the steep mass-luminosity relation or misstate the order of fusion stages.

items.prompt: Which observations count as evidence supporting the hot Big Bang model of the universe? Select all that apply.

options.label: Primordial helium and deuterium abundances match nucleosynthesis calculations
Pulsars slowly lose rotational energy and spin down over time
Distant galaxies show redshifts that rise with their distance
Mercury's perihelion precesses slightly faster than Newtonian gravity predicts
The cosmic microwave background has a near-perfect blackbody spectrum

rubric: The blackbody relic radiation, light-element abundances and redshift-distance relation each follow from a hot, expanding early universe.
Mercury's precession tests general relativity locally, and pulsar spin-down concerns neutron-star physics.

items.prompt: A student measures a galaxy's redshift as z = 0.002, giving a recession speed near 600 km/s. Cepheids place it at 3 Mpc. Using H0 = 70 km/s/Mpc, the student predicts 8.6 Mpc and concludes the Cepheid distance is wrong. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Both are wrong, because the relativistic Doppler formula changes the speed by a factor of three at this redshift
The Cepheid distance stands, because at 3 Mpc random peculiar velocities of hundreds of km/s rival the Hubble flow
Neither conflicts, because the Hubble law gives only a lower limit on distance, so 8.6 Mpc is simply allowed
The redshift distance stands, because Cepheids become unreliable beyond 1 Mpc and the 3 Mpc value must underestimate it

rubric: Nearby galaxies have peculiar velocities comparable to the small Hubble flow, so redshift is a poor distance guide there.
The distractors misjudge Cepheid range, misapply relativistic corrections at z = 0.002, or misread the Hubble law.

items.prompt: Transit data give a planet's radius and period. You must also find its bulk density with as little new observing as possible. Which addition completes the design?

options.label: A longer transit baseline, because tiny shifts in the period reveal the planet's mass without other observations
A second transit filter, because the change of depth with colour yields the planet's mass directly from the data
Radial velocity follow-up for mass, since the transit fixes inclination and density follows from mass and radius
Direct imaging, because the planet's reflected brightness gives its mass once the radius is known from transits

rubric: Transits fix inclination, so radial velocity amplitude gives true mass, and mass with radius gives density.
The distractors claim mass can be read from colour, period drift or brightness, which do not measure it directly.

items.prompt: Using a photometric survey of a globular cluster whose stars share one distance and one formation time, which plan would estimate its age?

options.label: Average the stars' radial velocities and divide the cluster radius by that speed
Measure the brightest star's pulsation period and apply the period-luminosity relation
Count red giants relative to main-sequence stars and convert the ratio to years
Plot a colour-magnitude diagram and fit isochrones to the main-sequence turnoff

rubric: The turnoff luminosity drops as a cluster ages, so fitting isochrones to it gives an age.
Pulsation periods give distance, crossing time is not age, and a giant-to-dwarf ratio is not calibrated to years.

items.prompt: You must image a faint galaxy from a light-polluted site. Constraints: the sky saturates a frame after 5 minutes, and the CCD has hot pixels and uneven illumination. Which plan works?

options.label: Take many short exposures and stack them without dithering, since calibration frames would add extra noise
Take many sub-5-minute dithered exposures, subtract darks, divide by flats, then stack
Take one 3-hour exposure for maximum signal, since calibration frames would only add noise to the result
Take a single 5-minute exposure and sharpen it heavily, since extra frames cannot add any detail at all

rubric: Short dithered frames avoid saturation, calibration removes hot pixels and illumination gradients, and stacking builds signal.
The distractors ignore saturation, skip calibration, or expect sharpening to replace integration time.

items.prompt: A proposal would measure the Hubble constant using periods and apparent magnitudes of Cepheids in distant galaxies with the period-luminosity relation. What is the design missing?

options.label: A spectrum of each Cepheid, from which its absolute magnitude can be read off directly
A zero point from Cepheids with geometric distances, such as parallax
A correction for the Sun's motion, which alone fixes the luminosity scale of the relation
A measurement of each host galaxy's age, which would set the luminosity scale of the variables

rubric: Without a geometric zero point, the period-luminosity relation gives only relative distances.
The distractors offer corrections that do not anchor absolute luminosity.

items.prompt: An asteroid's rotation period is expected to be between 2 and 6 hours. You will use photometry on a telescope. Which schedule meets the sampling constraints?

options.label: A continuous 10-hour run with one frame every 5 minutes
A continuous 2-hour run with one frame every minute, giving very fine detail of the light curve
One frame per night over 30 nights, enough to track any slow brightness change over a month
One frame every 3 hours over 2 nights, enough to catch at least a few points of each cycle

rubric: The run covers more than one full period at the longest expected value, and 5-minute sampling resolves the shortest.
The other schedules alias the period, undersample it, or cover less than one full cycle.

items.prompt: You must measure parallax of stars at 1 kpc (parallax 1 mas) to 10% accuracy, so the error must be 0.1 mas or less. Which designs meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Space astrometry with 0.5 mas precision per measurement, at epochs six months apart
Repeated 0.08 mas measurements over a year, fitted with a parallax and proper-motion model
A single ground-based exposure with 1 arcsec seeing, centroided to about a tenth of the seeing
Space astrometry with 0.05 mas precision per measurement, at epochs six months apart

rubric: Precision of 0.05 to 0.08 mas, with a baseline spanning the Earth's orbit, meets the 0.1 mas requirement.
0.5 mas is five times too coarse, and a single seeing-limited exposure gives 100 mas errors with no baseline.

items.prompt: A supernova appears in a galaxy 20 Mpc away. You have one night on a spectrograph and must decide whether it is Type Ia or core-collapse so the right follow-up can be chosen. Which plan meets this constraint?

options.label: Observe the host galaxy's colour, since elliptical hosts produce only Type Ia and spirals only core-collapse events
Record the peak brightness alone, since Type Ia events always reach the same absolute magnitude as other supernovae
Take a spectrum near peak and look for strong Si II absorption together with no hydrogen lines
Take a single colour image at peak, since Type Ia events are always redder than core-collapse events at maximum

rubric: Type Ia spectra show silicon absorption and lack hydrogen, so a spectrum separates them from most core-collapse events.
Host type, colour and peak brightness alone are unreliable, since both classes occur in varied settings and brightness differs.
